whyNext: Builds on contiguous subarray DP from Longest Turbulent Subarray (Seq 250) by incrementing running consecutive arithmetic lengths whenever nums[i] - nums[i-1] == nums[i-1] - nums[i-2], accumulating slices in O(n) time.
hints: An arithmetic slice must have length >= 3 and identical differences between adjacent elements.
If nums[i] - nums[i-1] == nums[i-1] - nums[i-2], then every arithmetic slice ending at index i - 1 can be extended to index i, plus one new slice of length 3 is formed: dp[i] = dp[i-1] + 1.
If the difference changes, the streak resets: dp[i] = 0. Accumulate sum of all dp[i] to get the total number of arithmetic slices.

brute.idea: Test every subarray nums[i..j] of length >= 3 to verify whether difference between adjacent elements remains constant.
steps: Loop i from 0 to n - 3.
Loop j from i + 2 to n - 1.
Check if diff = nums[k] - nums[k-1] is constant for all k in [i+1, j].
If constant, increment total slice count.
Return count.

optimal.idea: O(1) space contiguous DP: maintain current consecutive streak, accumulating into total sum in O(n) time.
steps: If nums.length < 3 return 0.
int curr = 0, total = 0;
Loop i from 2 to nums.length - 1: if nums[i] - nums[i-1] == nums[i-1] - nums[i-2]: curr++; total += curr; else curr = 0;
Return total.

whyNext: Builds on hash-map based subsequence state transition from Longest Increasing Subsequence (Seq 247) by storing the longest arithmetic subsequence length ending at value x as dp[x] = dp[x - difference] + 1 in O(n) time.
hints: Any element x can extend an arithmetic subsequence ending at x - difference.
Store dp[val] in a HashMap<Integer, Integer> representing the length of the longest subsequence ending at val.
For each num in arr: dp[num] = dp.getOrDefault(num - difference, 0) + 1. Track the maximum value in dp.

brute.idea: For each element, recursively search forward for the next element equal to cur + difference.
steps: For each starting index i from 0 to n - 1: initialize length = 1, target = arr[i] + difference.
Scan forward for matching elements and increment length.
Track maximum length found.
brute.whySlow: Scanning forward for every starting element takes O(n^2) time.

optimal.idea: HashMap dynamic programming: map each element x to 1 + dp[x - diff], running in O(n) single pass time.
steps: Map<Integer, Integer> dp = new HashMap<>(); int maxLen = 0;
For each x in arr: int prevLen = dp.getOrDefault(x - difference, 0); dp.put(x, prevLen + 1); maxLen = Math.max(maxLen, prevLen + 1);
Return maxLen.

whyNext: Generalizes fixed difference sequences from Longest Arithmetic Subsequence of Given Difference (Seq 474) to arbitrary differences by maintaining a 2D DP table dp[i][diff] of arithmetic subsequence lengths ending at index i with difference diff.
hints: Unlike the previous problem, the common difference is not fixed in advance.
Maintain dp[i][diff] representing the length of the longest arithmetic subsequence ending at index i with common difference diff.
For each pair (j, i) with j < i: diff = nums[i] - nums[j]. dp[i][diff] = dp[j].getOrDefault(diff, 1) + 1. Offset diff by 500 to store in flat array (or use array of HashMaps).

brute.idea: Check all pairs (i, j) to establish an initial difference, then search forward for all subsequent elements with that difference.
steps: Nested loop for first two elements nums[i] and nums[j].
Compute diff = nums[j] - nums[i].
Scan remaining elements for next terms in sequence.
Track maximum sequence length.
brute.whySlow: Checking all pairs and scanning forward takes O(n^3) time.

optimal.idea: 2D DP with difference indexing: dp[i][diff] = dp[j][diff] + 1 for each predecessor j < i, running in O(n^2) time.
steps: Let n = nums.length. Array values in [0, 500], so diff is in [-500, 500]. Offset by 500 to fit in [0, 1000].
int[][] dp = new int[n][1001]; int maxLen = 2;
For i from 0 to n - 1: for j from 0 to i - 1: diff = nums[i] - nums[j] + 500; dp[i][diff] = Math.max(dp[i][diff], (dp[j][diff] == 0 ? 1 : dp[j][diff]) + 1); maxLen = Math.max(maxLen, dp[i][diff]);
Return maxLen.

whyNext: Builds on LIS predecessor chaining from Longest Increasing Subsequence (Seq 247) by sorting nums and finding the longest chain where nums[i] % nums[j] == 0, reconstructing the subset via parent pointers.
hints: Sort nums ascending: if a divides b and b divides c, then a divides c transitively.
Maintain dp[i] as the size of the largest divisible subset ending at index i, and parent[i] pointing to the predecessor index.
For each i: for each j < i: if nums[i] % nums[j] == 0 and dp[j] + 1 > dp[i]: dp[i] = dp[j] + 1, parent[i] = j. Backtrack from the index with maximum dp to reconstruct the subset.

brute.idea: Generate all 2^n subsets, verify if every pair satisfies divisibility, and return the largest qualifying subset.
steps: Generate all possible subsets of nums.
Check each subset: for all pairs (a, b), verify a % b == 0 or b % a == 0.
Keep track of the largest valid subset.
Return largest subset found.

optimal.idea: Sort + LIS DP with parent pointer reconstruction: compute max subset in O(n^2) time and rebuild list in O(n) time.
steps: Sort nums ascending.
int[] dp = new int[n]; int[] parent = new int[n]; Arrays.fill(dp, 1); Arrays.fill(parent, -1);
int maxIdx = 0, maxVal = 1;
For i from 0 to n - 1: for j from 0 to i - 1: if nums[i] % nums[j] == 0 and dp[j] + 1 > dp[i]: dp[i] = dp[j] + 1; parent[i] = j; if dp[i] > maxVal: maxVal = dp[i]; maxIdx = i;
Reconstruct subset by following parent pointers from maxIdx.
Return subset list.

whyNext: Builds on multi-choice transition DP from Coin Change (Seq 242) by comparing 1-day, 7-day, and 30-day passes at each travel day to minimize cumulative transit cost.
hints: Track travel days using a boolean array or HashSet for O(1) travel day checks.
dp[d] represents minimum cost to travel up through day d (from day 1 to 365).
If day d is not a travel day, dp[d] = dp[d - 1]. If d is a travel day, dp[d] = min(dp[d - 1] + costs[0], dp[max(0, d - 7)] + costs[1], dp[max(0, d - 30)] + costs[2]).

brute.idea: Recursively choose 1-day, 7-day, or 30-day pass starting from the first travel day.
steps: Define dfs(dayIndex): if dayIndex >= days.length return 0.
Branch 1: buy 1-day pass, advance to next travel day.
Branch 2: buy 7-day pass, advance to first travel day >= days[dayIndex] + 7.
Branch 3: buy 30-day pass, advance to first travel day >= days[dayIndex] + 30.
Return minimum across the 3 branches.

optimal.idea: Calendar day DP: iterate from day 1 to lastDay, choosing min pass covering day d in O(lastDay) = O(1) time.
steps: boolean[] isTravel = new boolean[366]; for (int d : days) isTravel[d] = true;
int[] dp = new int[366];
For d from 1 to 365: if (!isTravel[d]) dp[d] = dp[d - 1]; else dp[d] = min(dp[d - 1] + costs[0], dp[max(0, d - 7)] + costs[1], dp[max(0, d - 30)] + costs[2]);
Return dp[days[days.length - 1]].

whyNext: Builds on skip-or-take backward DP from House Robber (Seq 238) by choosing between skipping question i (dp[i+1]) or solving it (points[i] + dp[i + brainpower[i] + 1]).
hints: Process questions backwards from index n - 1 down to 0.
At question i, you have two choices: skip it (score dp[i + 1]), or solve it (score points[i] + dp[next], where next = i + brainpower[i] + 1).
If next >= n, score from solving is simply points[i]. Set dp[i] = max(dp[i + 1], points[i] + (next < n ? dp[next] : 0)).

brute.idea: Forward recursion trying both choices (skip or solve) at each question.
steps: In dfs(i): if i >= n return 0.
skip = dfs(i + 1).
solve = points[i] + dfs(i + brainpower[i] + 1).
Return max(skip, solve).

optimal.idea: Backward 1D dynamic programming: compute dp[i] = max(dp[i + 1], points[i] + dp[i + brainpower[i] + 1]) in O(n) time.
steps: int n = questions.length; long[] dp = new long[n + 1];
Loop i from n - 1 down to 0: int next = i + questions[i][1] + 1; long solve = questions[i][0] + (next < n ? dp[next] : 0); dp[i] = Math.max(dp[i + 1], solve);
Return dp[0].

whyNext: Builds on target sum DP from Combination Sum IV (Seq 243) by rolling n identical k-sided dice to reach exact target sum modulo 10^9+7.
hints: dp[d][t] represents the number of ways to reach sum t using exactly d dice.
Base case: dp[0][0] = 1, all other dp[0][t] = 0.
For each die d from 1 to n: for each sum t from d to target: dp[d][t] = sum(dp[d - 1][t - face]) for face in [1, k] where t - face >= 0, modulo 10^9+7.

brute.idea: Recursive backtracking: roll each die choosing face from 1 to k, counting paths that total target.
steps: In dfs(diceLeft, targetLeft): if diceLeft == 0 return targetLeft == 0 ? 1 : 0.
Sum dfs(diceLeft - 1, targetLeft - face) for face from 1 to k.
Return sum modulo 10^9+7.

optimal.idea: 2D / 1D rolling array dynamic programming: dp[t] = sum(prevDp[t - face]) in O(n * target * k) time.
steps: int MOD = 1_000_000_007; int[] dp = new int[target + 1]; dp[0] = 1;
For die from 1 to n: int[] nextDp = new int[target + 1];
For t from die to target: for face from 1 to min(k, t): nextDp[t] = (nextDp[t] + dp[t - face]) % MOD;
dp = nextDp; Return dp[target].

whyNext: Builds on 2D 0-1 Knapsack from Target Sum (Seq 251) by extending knapsack capacity to two independent resource constraints: m zeros and n ones.
hints: Each string costs zeros 0s and ones 1s, and yields a value of 1 string.
dp[i][j] represents the maximum number of strings formed using at most i zeros and j ones.
Traverse backwards to reuse 2D array: for i from m down to zeros: for j from n down to ones: dp[i][j] = max(dp[i][j], dp[i - zeros][j - ones] + 1).

brute.idea: Recursively decide to take or skip each string, tracking consumed zeros and ones.
steps: In dfs(idx, zerosLeft, onesLeft): if idx == strs.length return 0.
skip = dfs(idx + 1, zerosLeft, onesLeft).
Count zeros and ones in strs[idx]. If affordable, take = 1 + dfs(idx + 1, zerosLeft - zeros, onesLeft - ones).
Return max(skip, take).

optimal.idea: 2D backward knapsack DP: update dp[i][j] from (m, n) down to (zeros, ones) in O(L * m * n) time.
steps: int[][] dp = new int[m + 1][n + 1];
For each string s: count zeros and ones in s.
For i from m down to zeros: for j from n down to ones: dp[i][j] = Math.max(dp[i][j], dp[i - zeros][j - ones] + 1);
Return dp[m][n].

whyNext: Builds on recurrence relations from Climbing Stairs (Seq 235) by modeling state transitions across fully covered and partially covered 2xn grid columns (dp[i] = 2*dp[i-1] + dp[i-3]).
hints: Track full tilings and partial tilings with one square sticking out.
Full tiling recurrence simplifies to: dp[i] = (2 * dp[i - 1] + dp[i - 3]) % 10^9+7.
Base cases: dp[0] = 1, dp[1] = 1, dp[2] = 2, dp[3] = 5. Compute iteratively up to n.

brute.idea: Mutual state recursion: full(n) calls full and partial state transitions recursively.
steps: full(n) = full(n-1) + full(n-2) + 2*partial(n-1).
partial(n) = full(n-2) + partial(n-1).
Compute with memoization modulo 10^9+7.
brute.whySlow: Mutual recursion with two state functions.

optimal.idea: Single simplified recurrence relation dp[i] = 2*dp[i-1] + dp[i-3] in O(n) time and O(1) space.
steps: If n <= 1 return 1; if n == 2 return 2; if n == 3 return 5.
Rolling variables: p3 = 1, p2 = 1, p1 = 2, cur = 5.
Loop i from 4 to n: next = (2 * cur + p3) % MOD; p3 = p2; p2 = p1; p1 = cur; cur = next;
Return (int) cur.

whyNext: Builds on partition window decisions from Solving Questions With Brainpower (Seq 478) by trying each partition size len from 1 to k, changing all elements in the window to max(window) to maximize total sum.
hints: dp[i] represents the maximum sum possible partitioning the prefix arr[0..i-1].
For each index i from 1 to n: consider the last partition starting at index i - len for len in [1, k].
Track maxVal in the window arr[i - len..i - 1]. dp[i] = max(dp[i], dp[i - len] + maxVal * len).

brute.idea: Recursive backtracking trying all partition lengths from 1 to k starting from index 0.
steps: In dfs(i): if i == n return 0.
Loop len from 1 to min(k, n - i).
Track max in arr[i..i+len-1].
Take max of maxVal * len + dfs(i + len).
Return best sum.

optimal.idea: Forward 1D DP with k-window scanning: dp[i] = max(dp[i - len] + maxVal * len) in O(n * k) time.
steps: int n = arr.length; int[] dp = new int[n + 1];
For i from 1 to n: int maxVal = 0;
For len from 1 to min(k, i): maxVal = max(maxVal, arr[i - len]); dp[i] = max(dp[i], dp[i - len] + maxVal * len);
Return dp[n].

whyNext: Builds on modular remainder states from Target Sum (Seq 251) by maintaining maximum subarray sums under modulo 3 (reminders 0, 1, 2) in O(n) time.
hints: dp[r] represents the maximum sum achieved so far with sum % 3 == r.
Initialize dp[0] = 0, dp[1] = -infinity, dp[2] = -infinity.
For each num: clone dp into next; for r in {0, 1, 2}: next[(r + num) % 3] = max(next[(r + num) % 3], dp[r] + num). Set dp = next. Return dp[0].

brute.idea: Compute total sum; if total % 3 != 0, find and remove smallest elements with remainder 1 or 2.
steps: Calculate total sum.
Sort elements with rem 1 and rem 2.
If sum % 3 == 1: remove 1 smallest from rem1, or 2 smallest from rem2.
If sum % 3 == 2: remove 1 smallest from rem2, or 2 smallest from rem1.
Return maximum resulting sum.
brute.whySlow: Requires collecting and sorting modulo buckets.

optimal.idea: 3-state modular DP: dp[0, 1, 2] tracks maximum sum with remainder r, running in O(n) time and O(1) space.
steps: For each x in nums: int[] next = dp.clone(); for r in 0..2: next[(r + x) % 3] = max(next[(r + x) % 3], dp[r] + x); dp = next;
Return dp[0].

whyNext: Builds on Kadane's maximum subarray algorithm from Maximum Subarray (Seq 176) by maintaining two states: noDel (max subarray ending at i without deletion) and oneDel (max subarray ending at i with exactly one deletion).
hints: noDel is standard Kadane: noDel = max(num, noDel + num).
oneDel can either delete current num (inheriting previous noDel) or keep current num after an earlier deletion: oneDel = max(prevNoDel, oneDel + num).
Update global max with max(noDel, oneDel) at each step.

brute.idea: Compute standard Kadane's sum, then test deleting each element one by one and finding max subarray.
steps: Compute max subarray sum without any deletion.
For each index i: test removing nums[i], compute Kadane's algorithm on remaining array.
Return maximum found.

code.python:
class Solution:
    def maximumSum(self, arr: list[int]) -> int:
        n = len(arr)
        max_val = max(arr)
        if max_val < 0:
            return max_val
        no_del = arr[0]
        one_del = 0
        res = arr[0]
        for i in range(1, n):
            one_del = max(no_del, one_del + arr[i])
            no_del = max(arr[i], no_del + arr[i])
            res = max(res, no_del, one_del)
        return res

optimal.idea: 2-state Kadane dynamic programming: track noDel and oneDel in O(1) space and O(n) linear time.
steps: int noDel = arr[0], oneDel = 0, ans = arr[0];
For i from 1 to arr.length - 1: int x = arr[i]; oneDel = max(noDel, oneDel + x); noDel = max(x, noDel + x); ans = max(ans, max(noDel, oneDel));
Return ans.

code.python:
class Solution:
    def maximumSum(self, arr: list[int]) -> int:
        no_del = arr[0]
        one_del = 0
        ans = arr[0]
        for i in range(1, len(arr)):
            x = arr[i]
            one_del = max(no_del, one_del + x)
            no_del = max(x, no_del + x)
            ans = max(ans, no_del, one_del)
        return ans

whyNext: Builds on interval scheduling from Non-overlapping Intervals (Seq 424) by associating each interval with a profit and finding the maximum profit subset of non-overlapping jobs using sorting, DP, and binary search.
hints: Combine startTime, endTime, and profit into job objects and sort them by endTime.
Define dp[i] as the maximum profit achievable considering a subset of the first i jobs.
For job i, either skip it (dp[i-1]) or take it: add its profit to dp[j], where j is the latest job finishing on or before job i starts, found via binary search.

brute.idea: Recursively explore all subsets of mutually non-overlapping jobs and track the maximum profit.
steps: Sort jobs by start time.
Use recursion: at each job, decide whether to include it (if compatible with the previous included job) or skip it.
Track max profit across all valid combination paths.
Return maximum profit.

optimal.idea: Sort jobs by end time and use dynamic programming with binary search to find the latest non-conflicting job in O(n log n) time.
steps: Combine startTime, endTime, and profit into a 2D array and sort by endTime ascending.
Create dp array where dp[i] is the max profit using a subset of the first i jobs (1-indexed).
For job i (0-indexed): binary search for the largest j (0 to i-1) where jobs[j].endTime <= jobs[i].startTime.
dp[i+1] = max(dp[i], jobs[i].profit + dp[j+1]).
Return dp[n].

whyNext: Builds on single-string prefix parsing from Decode Ways (Seq 241) by introducing the wildcard character '*' which can represent any digit 1-9, requiring case-by-case transition counting modulo 10^9+7.
hints: Track dp[i]: the number of decodings for prefix s[0..i).
Single char transitions: '1'-'9' give 1 way; '*' gives 9 ways; '0' gives 0 ways.
Two char transitions: analyze s[i-2] and s[i-1] considering digits and '*' (e.g., '**' can form 11-19 and 21-26, giving 15 combinations; '*7' gives 2 ways: 17, 27).

brute.idea: Recursively branch on 1-digit and 2-digit interpretations, expanding '*' to all possible valid digits 1-9.
steps: Recursive function dfs(idx) returns number of ways to decode from idx.
If idx == s.length(), return 1.
Branch on 1-digit possibilities (1-9 or '*' -> 9).
Branch on 2-digit possibilities (10-26 or '*' expanding).
Sum valid branches modulo 10^9 + 7.

optimal.idea: Space-optimized dynamic programming maintaining the previous two decoding counts modulo 10^9+7.
steps: Initialize prev2 = 1 (empty string), prev1 = ways to decode s[0].
For each index i from 1 to n-1: calculate 1-character transition count and 2-character transition count.
curr = (ways1 * prev1 + ways2 * prev2) % 1_000_000_007.
Shift variables: prev2 = prev1, prev1 = curr.
Return (int) prev1.
